newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania ruling party seeks to deflect pyramid fury.
newsitem.headline: Albania ruling party seeks to deflect pyramid fury.

text.p: Albania's ruling right-wing Democrats, seeking to deflate public anger over the collapse of hugely popular pyramid investment schemes, called a rally for Tuesday to denounce rioting which has swept the country.
In an apparent bid to avoid any escalation of violence, the government party dropped original plans to stage the protest outside the headquarters of the opposition Socialist party.
Ministers have accused the Socialists of fanning unrest over the failure of the high-yielding schemes in which many Albanians had poured their life savings.
Instead the Democrats called on its supporters to gather at the town hall (1100 GMT), which they say was damaged by protesters on Sunday during clashes with riot police.

"The Democratic party has decided to change the rally... into a constructive rally against violence and destruction by calling on its sympathisers in the capital to repair the damage caused to Tirana town hall," Albanian state television said.

The town hall is on one side of Tirana's huge central Skanderbeg Square across from the main offices of the Socialists, successors of the old communist party that ruled Albania for more than 40 years until 1990.

On the eve of the government rally, a senior figure in the Socialist party and former member of parliament, Ndre Legisi, suffered a fractured skull after he was attacked by three or four men near the centre of Tirana.
Doctors said Legisi was in a critical condition. The motives for the attack were not immediately clear.
Albanian President Sali Berisha, founder of the Democratic party, deployed troops around the country on Sunday after the weekend confrontations.

Armed soldiers surrounded the central bank and guarded state television headquarters in the capital while Radio Tirana reported that troops began clearing roads near flashpoints where protesters had erected barricades to prevent police reinforcements reaching their towns.
The president said on Monday he saw no need to call a state of emergency and added that the troops would only be used for a limited period to replace policemen injured in the clashes.
Economists estimate that almost all Albanians are directly, or indirectly affected by the collapse of the pyramid schemes, with many people facing financial ruin.
In an attempt to appease desperate investors, Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi pledged to pay Albanians all the money they have put in failed schemes with bank interest starting from February 5.
Authorities have frozen some $300 million placed in state banks by two pyramid operators but the sum was unlikely to be enough to compensate everyone affected.
Pyramid schemes took off in Albania after the overthrow of the communist regime, with some private funds promising to double people's investments in two or three months.
Economists think more than $1.0 billion was sunk into the funds and say Meksi will be hard pushed to pay back the money.
"The only way the government can compensate people in full is by printing money and that will set inflation alight," said Zef Preci, director of the independent Albanian Centre for Economic Research.
